tip_title: One Winter Prep Step That Could Keep a Claim Off Your Record Entirely
topic: Winter Storm Home Insurance - Winterization and Claims Avoidance
blurb:
💡 **Insurance Tip: One Winter Prep Step That Could Keep a Claim Off Your Record Entirely**

Most of the winter storm insurance coverage we talk about is about what gets paid after something goes wrong. But there's a winterization step worth doing right now that's really about keeping damage from happening in the first place: checking your attic insulation and making sure heat is circulating to exterior walls where pipes run. When a pipe freezes and bursts because the home wasn't adequately heated or insulated, insurers typically treat that as a maintenance issue rather than a sudden loss — which can mean a denied claim. The easier path is sealing drafts, confirming your heat is set above 55 degrees if you're leaving for the holiday, and asking a neighbor to check on things if you'll be away.

If you do end up with a winter damage situation and you're not sure how your policy handles it, your Peachy agent can walk through the specifics with you before you call in a claim.

📖 [Learn more from Investopedia](https://www.investopedia.com/winter-storms-and-home-insurance-what-every-homeowner-needs-to-know-8779358)
summary: Covers proactive winterization steps (attic insulation, pipe heat, home-unoccupied protocol) as a claims-avoidance strategy framed around the maintenance exclusion in homeowners policies, distinct from prior tips on what winter damage is or isn't covered after the fact.
scoring_notes: Late November is exactly when Georgia homeowners leave for Thanksgiving travel and risk coming home to a freeze event. Prior winter tips (Nov 2, Nov 9, Nov 13, Nov 16) covered what's covered/not covered, documentation steps, ice dams, pipe freeze mechanics, and space heaters. This tip takes a genuinely different angle: what to do before anything happens to avoid tripping the maintenance exclusion entirely, with a specific 'leaving for the holiday' hook. 78% homeowner audiences in both newsletters make this broadly applicable. Source is Investopedia — not on the preferred trusted list, but it's a credible personal finance publisher and no preferred-list source had this exact angle in the candidates. Acceptable given the HARD MINIMUM requirement and the strong seasonal fit.

tip_title: Thanksgiving Is Days Away. Here's the One Thing Most Hosts Never Think to Check.
topic: Home Insurance - Holiday Hosting Liability and Premises Coverage
blurb:
💡 **Insurance Tip: Thanksgiving Is Days Away. Here's the One Thing Most Hosts Never Think to Check.**

When you've got family and friends in the house for the holidays, your personal liability coverage is quietly doing a job most people don't think about until something goes wrong. If a guest slips on a wet floor, trips on the front steps, or gets hurt in some other way on your property, your homeowners policy's liability coverage is what responds first. The question worth asking before Thursday is whether the limit on your policy still makes sense for the household you have today, not the one you had when you first bought coverage. A lot of people set that number once and never look at it again.

Not sure what your liability limit is or whether it's still the right number? Your Peachy agent can pull it up and walk you through it in a few minutes.

📖 [Learn more from the Insurance Information Institute](https://www.iii.org/article/insuring-your-home-based-business)
summary: Covers personal liability coverage on homeowners policies framed around Thanksgiving holiday hosting, specifically the risk of guest injuries on the property and whether the existing liability limit is still adequate for today's household.
scoring_notes: Thanksgiving is literally days away from November 20 — peak hosting relevance. Prior liability tips (Aug 24, Sep 7, Sep 11) covered the default $100k limit number, the three liability tiers, and the scenario-level claims walkthrough. This tip takes a fresh angle: the holiday-hosting prompt to check whether the number is still right for the current household, not a first-time education moment. High homeownership rates in both audiences (78%+) means virtually the whole readership is a potential host. Actionable this week.
